title: Sedentary breaks in daily life: Investigating between- and within-person effects for optimizing just-in-time-adaptive interventions
summary:
Prolonged sedentary behavior in daily life, for example at work, is linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease, diabetes and depression. The World Health Organization therefore recommends regularly interrupting long periods of sitting with physical activity. However, little is known about how often, how long and how intensely such breaks should be.
In this study, we test how smartphone reminders should be designed so that people sit less in everyday life. Healthy adults who sit a lot wear a small motion sensor on the thigh. The sensor detects whether a person is sitting or standing and sends this information to a smartphone.
In the first part (160 participants, 2 weeks), participants are randomly assigned to different reminder variants: 4 or 8 times a day, for light or brisker activity, for 3 or 10 minutes, triggered by the sensor after prolonged sitting or partly at random times. This shows which combination works best.
In the second part (60 participants, 4 weeks), the best combination is tested in an app. We also test whether feedback on one's own sitting behavior and motivational messages help. Before the study starts, participants attend one lab session with questionnaires and short computer tasks. The results will help design future health apps that offer support at exactly the right moment.
conditions: Lack of physical activity; Sedentary behavior (prolonged uninterrupted sitting) in daily life

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Age 18–65 years
• Predominantly sedentary daily routine (e.g. office work)
• Sufficient German language skills to follow lab instructions and answer smartphone prompts
• Written informed consent (consent and data protection declaration)
Exclusion criteria:
• Current illness or injury that would restrict the lab assessment, the smartphone prompts or daily activity
• Current (diagnosed) mental disorder
